newsitem.title: USA: Larger crops projected in U.S., other key regions.
newsitem.headline: Larger crops projected in U.S., other key regions.

text.p: The Agriculture Department on Friday raised its estimates for this year's U.S. corn and soybean crops and hiked its projections for crop output in many key growing areas throughout the world.
The department said U.S. corn production will hit 9.01 billion bushels, up from its previous estimate of 8.804 billion bushels and the third-largest corn crop on record.
The largest corn harvest in U.S. history was recorded in 1994 at 10.1 billion bushels.
Soybean production was pegged at 2.35 billion bushels, up from the agency's September estimate of 2.270 billion and the second-largest American soybean crop ever.
Corn and soybean futures prices dropped sharply at the Chicago Board of Trade, the world's largest commodity exchange, in response to the report.
Soybean contracts dropped by as much as 30 cents per bushel, and corn prices slipped by up to 7-1/2 cents.
"There's nothing friendly about the corn or bean numbers," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities in Chicago.
"Those are big numbers, the crop's getting bigger," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.
The U.S. corn crop is a sharp improvement from last year's poor harvest of 7.374 billion bushels and will help replenish stocks that have dropped to unprecedented low levels.

Surplus corn stocks are projected to total around 900 million bushels by next fall, more than double the ending stocks level this fall, but still some 40 percent below the available supply of 1.6 billion bushels of corn at this time last year.
Important major growing areas outside the United States also will see abundant harvests this year, said the agency, which will likely cut into U.S. agricultural exports.
"It should be a difficult export market this year and next," said an analyst with a major exporting company.

Corn and wheat are the country's two biggest export crops. U.S. corn exports account for two-thirds of the corn traded in world markets, while U.S.-grown wheat makes up more than a quarter of the wheat traded globally.

Wheat harvests in the major exporting countries of Australia and the European Union were raised Friday from last month's estimates, and the projected wheat harvest from Canada, America's top wheat competitor, was kept unchanged at a bumper level.

Big wheat importing nations, notably China and North African countries, were also projected to have bumper crops. The Chinese wheat harvest was raised to 109 million metric tons, and North Africa wheat production was left unchanged at the high level of almost 16 million tons.
Corn production outside the United States was also projected at high levels.

China, North Africa, Europe and Mexico -- all big buyers of U.S. corn -- will harvest big, if not record, corn crops this year. The Agriculture Department increased its estimate for Chinese corn production to 117 million tons, a record level.
Grain analysts said the more abundant crops will increase competition in the global grain market as exporters with abundant supplies fight for the smaller market share.
"For the business that will be out there, it will be tough competition," said Dale Gustafson, senior grains and oilseed analyst with Smith Barney.
Agricultural experts said that the slower export pace will most likely dampen crop prices next year. Prices have been on a roller coaster ride for months because of the low stocks.
